title: How To Limit Your Students’ Screen Time
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Citing American Heart Association data that children already spend over seven hours a day on screens even before pandemic-driven online schooling, Linsin argues that teachers can meaningfully reduce that burden by shifting the balance of a lesson toward offline independent work. He lays out a five-step structure: teach one objective, keep the direct-instruction portion brief, check for understanding via a quick camera-held-up proof, ensure students work with cameras on so the teacher can monitor, and have students complete the actual work using pencil and paper rather than a screen. He recommends a 1:4 ratio of screen-based instruction time to offline independent work time, arguing this simultaneously cuts screen exposure and accelerates learning by building stamina, focus, and motivation.
points: Children already average over seven hours of daily screen time, a figure worsened by pandemic online schooling.
Teach one clear objective per lesson and keep direct instruction brief to avoid losing students to distraction.
Use a quick camera-held-up check for understanding before releasing students to independent work.
Have students complete assigned work with pencil and paper rather than on a screen whenever possible.
Aim for roughly a 1:4 ratio of teacher instruction time to student independent work time.
quotes: According to the American Heart Association, children ages 8-18 spend an average of more than 7 hours a day on their phones, playing video games, or watching TV.
This underscores the importance for us to do our part in limiting their screen time.
While online in particular, you must, must, must teach lessons that show students one thing they must be able to do or know.
Have them complete their work using good ol’ lead and timber—which has unique benefits that we’ll also cover in the future—while you observe from your end.
I recommend a ratio of 1:4—that is, your lesson to their independent work time. This way, you cut way down on their screen time while at the same time accelerating improvement.
Most critical, however, at least when it comes to their long-term health, it gets students offline.
